provenance.other: “Perfect understanding” occurs in exactly one KJV verse, Luke 1:3. The Book of Mormon adds an indefinite article — “a man of a perfect understanding” — and the fuller string “a perfect understanding” occurs in no KJV verse, so the borrowing is of the collocation and not of a clause.
provenance.significance: Luke 1:3 is the King James Bible's one sentence in which a writer explains his qualifications for compiling a record: having had perfect understanding of all things from the very first, he will write in order for Theophilus. The phrase belongs to a historian's preface, not to a soldier. Alma 48 is the Book of Mormon's most conspicuous compiler's intrusion — Mormon stopping his narrative to say what kind of man Moroni was, and, seven verses later, to say what would have happened to the powers of hell if all men had been like him — and the compliment he reaches for is the phrase the KJV gives to the evangelist introducing his own abridgment. The suppressed correspondence is between the two abridgers rather than between Moroni and Luke: the one place the King James Bible praises a man for perfect understanding is the place a writer is vouching for the reliability of what follows.

48:11.note: “He was a man of a perfect understanding.” Two words, one KJV verse, and a wholly different register in each: a Gospel preface against a general's obituary. It is an allusion rather than an echo because the collocation is genuinely distinctive — the KJV pairs “perfect” with “understanding” nowhere else — and moderate rather than high because two words plus an added article is a slender base and the phrase is unremarkable English on its own. Far below Skousen's sixteen-word threshold.
48:11.whyNot: “Perfect understanding” is an ordinary compliment in nineteenth-century English and needs no biblical model; the KJV's single occurrence may say more about how rarely the King James translators used the word “perfect” of an intellect than about where Alma 48:11 got its phrase.
48:11.text: It seemed good to me also, having had perfect understanding of all things from the very first, to write unto thee in order, most excellent Theophilus,

provenance.other: “Delight in war” occurs in exactly one KJV verse, Psalm 68:30 — “scatter thou the people that delight in war.” The Book of Mormon's object is different: “did not delight in bloodshed” here, “not in the shedding of blood” at 48:16, “they did not delight in the shedding of blood” at 48:23. That last is the psalm's verb married to the noun phrase of Hebrews 9:22, which this catalogue adjudicates at Alma 34:13 and carries as a composite at Alma 24:17.
provenance.significance: Psalm 68:30 is a prayer that God scatter the warlike, and it is the King James Bible's only use of “delight” with war as its object. Alma 48 states the negative of it three times in fifteen verses, of the man who is at that moment fortifying every city in the land. The chapter's whole difficulty — a book praising a general for not being warlike — is the psalm's category being invoked in order to be denied, and the denial is what licenses everything Moroni then does. Recover the psalm's context and the prayer is for the scattering of the nations that come against Israel, which is precisely the position Moroni's enemies occupy and precisely the position he is at pains not to occupy himself.

48:11.note: “A man that did not delight in bloodshed”, and again at 48:16 and 48:23. The collocation the Book of Mormon is negating stands in one KJV verse, and its object there is war rather than blood; the Book of Mormon substitutes the noun phrase of Hebrews 9:22. Held at echo because neither element is reproduced intact and the sentiment is available without a source, and at moderate because the triple repetition inside one chapter is the shape of a writer working from a phrase rather than reaching a thought twice.
48:11.whyNot: Nobody needs Psalm 68 to say that a good man does not enjoy killing. The row rests on a single verb-plus-object collocation whose KJV rarity may be an accident of the psalter's vocabulary, and a reader who declines it loses nothing from the chapter.
48:11.text: Rebuke the company of spearmen, the multitude of the bulls, with the calves of the people, till every one submit himself with pieces of silver: scatter thou the people that delight in war.

provenance.other: “Sworn with an oath” occurs in exactly one KJV verse, Acts 2:30, and the Book of Mormon reproduces the four words without change: “he had sworn with an oath, to defend his people.” The phrase returns at Alma 49:17 of the Lamanite chief captains, which is the same book and the same narrator's formula.
provenance.significance: In Acts 2:30 the swearer is God and the oath is the Davidic promise — Peter at Pentecost, arguing from Psalm 132 that God bound himself by oath to set Christ on David's throne. It is the King James Bible's one solemn-oath formula, and it belongs to a promise about a king. Alma 48:13 puts it in the mouth of the man who has just prevented one: Moroni swears, in his own person, to defend “his people, his rights, and his country, and his religion, even to the loss of his blood”, in the chapter after a usurper took a throne by fraud. The oath that in Acts establishes a monarchy here underwrites a republic. Note also what the borrowing does to 49:17, where the Lamanite captains swear with the same oath to take a city: the formula is applied to both sides, and the Book of Mormon does not mark the difference — the difference is in what is sworn to.

48:13.note: Four consecutive words reproducing the King James Bible's only oath-formula of this shape, in the chapter's most formal sentence. The catalogue's row for the second Alma occurrence is at 49:17; this is the first use in the book and carries the argument. Not a quotation and well below Skousen's threshold, but the string is exact and the source is unique.
48:13.text: Therefore being a prophet, and knowing that God had sworn with an oath to him, that of the fruit of his loins, according to the flesh, he would raise up Christ to sit on his throne;

provenance.other: “Give none offence” occurs in exactly one KJV verse, 1 Corinthians 10:32 — “Give none offence, neither to the Jews, nor to the Gentiles, nor to the church of God.” Alma 48:14 has “they were also taught never to give an offence”, with the KJV's verb and its object and a negative adverb for the KJV's negative determiner. This catalogue already carries 1 Corinthians 10:32 as a composite at Alma 4:10, where the shared material is Paul's stumblingblock argument rather than this phrase.
provenance.significance: Paul's rule is about the table and the conscience of a watching outsider: do not let your liberty be the thing that trips a Jew, a Gentile, or the church. Alma 48:14 makes it a rule of war. “Never to give an offence; yea, and never to raise the sword, except it were against an enemy” — the second clause glosses the first, so that giving offence now means striking first. Recover Paul's context and the transposition is doing real work: the Nephite doctrine of the defensive war is grounded in an apostolic rule about not being a stumblingblock, which is why the chapter can insist in the same breath that Moroni fortified every city and that his people never gave offence. The word “offence” carries its Pauline sense of an occasion of stumbling into a sentence about who may draw a sword first.

48:14.note: A KJV singleton, reproduced with the verb and object intact, in the sentence that states the Book of Mormon's doctrine of defensive war. The catalogue's earlier row at Alma 4:10 uses this verse for its stumblingblock clause; the phrase itself is borrowed here, and the two uses are different enough that the row is written rather than cross-referenced. Moderate rather than high because three words is a slender base and “give offence” had long since passed into ordinary English independent of Paul.
48:14.whyNot: “Give offence” is common English and the KJV's single occurrence of the imperative may be incidental; the Book of Mormon's sentence would read the same if no biblical rule stood behind it, and its own following clause about the sword supplies all the sense the passage needs.
48:14.text: Give none offence, neither to the Jews, nor to the Gentiles, nor to the church of God:

48:24.text: Hereby perceive we the love of God, because he laid down his life for us: and we ought to lay down our lives for the brethren.

provenance.other: “Lay down our lives” occurs in exactly one KJV verse, 1 John 3:16 — “we ought to lay down our lives for the brethren” — and it is the King James Bible's only plural of the idiom; the singular “lay down his life” is likewise a singleton, at John 15:13. Alma 48:24 has “they could not suffer to lay down their lives”, which is the plural with a third-person pronoun and a negative. “Lay down their lives” with that pronoun occurs in no KJV verse.
provenance.significance: 1 John 3:16 states the duty in the plural and names its beneficiaries: we ought to lay down our lives for the brethren. Alma 48:24 refuses it, and refuses it on a ground the epistle does not consider — “they could not suffer to lay down their lives, that their wives and their children should be massacred by the barbarous cruelty of those who was once their brethren.” The word “brethren” is in both sentences and it has changed sides: in the epistle the brethren are whom you die for, and in Alma 48:24 the brethren are the dissenters who would do the killing. That is the chapter's whole moral problem in one clause, and the borrowing is what makes it visible. Compare Hays on metalepsis — the suppressed term is the epistle's next verse, on shutting up one's bowels of compassion from a brother in need, which is exactly the charge the Nephites are anticipating against themselves for taking up arms.

48:24.note: “They could not suffer to lay down their lives, that their wives and their children should be massacred.” The King James Bible forms this plural once, and it forms it as a command; Alma 48:24 forms it as an impossibility. Held at moderate rather than high because the idiom had long been ordinary English and the negative construction is the Book of Mormon's own, but the plural and the shared noun “brethren” are more than the singular Johannine tag would give. The catalogue's other row for this verse is at Alma 53:17, where the pledge is made rather than declined; this is the first use in the book and carries the argument.
48:24.whyNot: “Lay down one's life” is thoroughly naturalized English and no writer needs 1 John to reach it, and Alma 48:24's sentence is a negation, which is the weakest kind of verbal contact. A reader may hold that the catalogue has found a common idiom and read an inversion into an accident.
